bio-001.why: Statins occupy the substrate-binding site of 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-CoA (HMG-CoA) reductase. By competing with HMG-CoA, they reduce mevalonate production and slow cholesterol synthesis in the liver.

notes.B: AMP-activated protein kinase can phosphorylate and inhibit the reductase when cellular energy is scarce.
notes.C: An upstream kinase activates AMP-activated protein kinase, placing it a step removed from the enzyme that binds statins.
notes.D: The phosphatase removes an inhibitory phosphate from the reductase, restoring its activity independently of statin binding.
notes.E: Protein kinase A transmits signals from cyclic AMP, whereas statins bind the enzyme that produces mevalonate.

bio-002.why: When cellular energy is scarce, AMP-activated protein kinase phosphorylates HMG-CoA reductase. This reduces the production of mevalonate and slows the energy-consuming synthesis of cholesterol.

notes.A: The reductase converts HMG-CoA into mevalonate and receives its inhibitory phosphate from a separate kinase.
notes.C: An upstream kinase activates AMP-activated protein kinase, which then directly phosphorylates the reductase.
notes.D: The phosphatase removes the inhibitory phosphate from HMG-CoA reductase, allowing cholesterol synthesis to resume.
notes.E: Protein kinase A responds to cyclic AMP, whereas the enzyme that directly senses energy status and inhibits the reductase is AMP-activated protein kinase.

bio-003.why: An upstream kinase phosphorylates a threonine in the catalytic subunit of AMP-activated protein kinase. This phosphorylation allows the energy sensor to inhibit biosynthetic pathways when energy is scarce.

notes.A: HMG-CoA reductase makes mevalonate and is a downstream target of the activated energy sensor.
notes.B: AMP-activated protein kinase is the enzyme receiving the activating phosphate in this signalling step.
notes.D: The reductase phosphatase restores the activity of the cholesterol-synthesis enzyme by removing its inhibitory phosphate.
notes.E: Protein kinase A responds to cyclic AMP, whereas a distinct upstream kinase phosphorylates the activation loop of the energy sensor.

bio-005.why: Acetyl-CoA carboxylase uses ATP, bicarbonate and the cofactor biotin to convert acetyl-CoA to malonyl-CoA. This commits carbon to fatty acid synthesis and controls the supply of two-carbon units for elongation.

notes.A: Condensation takes place on fatty acid synthase once the carboxylase has supplied the malonyl group.
notes.B: Acetate can be activated to acetyl-CoA, but this also supplies pathways other than fatty acid synthesis.
notes.C: The carboxylase adds bicarbonate-derived carbon to acetyl-CoA, so free malonate is not its starting material.
notes.E: The first reduction on fatty acid synthase consumes NADPH after the chain has already undergone condensation.

bio-006.why: A sustained carbohydrate surplus can provide acetyl-CoA for new fatty acids and glycerol 3-phosphate for their storage as triacylglycerol. Insulin promotes fatty acid synthesis and esterification in the fed state.

notes.A: Plants also synthesise triacylglycerols, which are an important energy reserve in many seeds.
notes.C: Low carbohydrate availability generally favours oxidation of fatty acids and reduces the use of carbohydrate carbon for new fatty acids.
notes.D: Animals synthesise triacylglycerols in the fed state, including in the liver and adipose tissue.
notes.E: A sustained carbohydrate surplus supplies both carbon and an insulin signal for fat storage in humans.

bio-007.why: Insulin favours storage after a carbohydrate-rich meal. Glucose supplies glycerol 3-phosphate for the triacylglycerol backbone and can supply acetyl-CoA for synthesis of the attached fatty acids.

notes.A: Fat is stored with little water and yields more energy per gram than hydrated glycogen.
notes.C: Insulin promotes fatty acid synthesis and storage after feeding, while low insulin favours release of fatty acids from adipose tissue.
notes.D: Mammalian liver can convert surplus glucose into fatty acids and esterify these to form triacylglycerols.
notes.E: Phosphatidate loses its phosphate to form diacylglycerol, which receives a third fatty acyl group.

bio-008.why: In the cytidine diphosphate (CDP) routes, one partner is activated and the other supplies a free hydroxyl group. Linking two CDP-activated partners is unnecessary for forming the phosphodiester bond.

notes.A: CDP-choline transfers its phosphocholine group to diacylglycerol during the formation of phosphatidylcholine.
notes.B: Free inositol reacts with activated CDP-diacylglycerol in the pathway that forms phosphatidylinositol.
notes.D: Mammalian cells can exchange serine for the ethanolamine head group of phosphatidylethanolamine to make phosphatidylserine.
notes.E: The liver can synthesise phosphatidylcholine by adding three methyl groups to the head group of phosphatidylethanolamine.

bio-009.why: Low-density lipoprotein carries much of the cholesterol in plasma as cholesteryl esters. Cells can bind its apolipoprotein B-100 through LDL receptors and take up the particle by endocytosis.

notes.A: Intermediate-density lipoprotein is a remnant that can return to the liver or give rise to low-density lipoprotein.
notes.C: High-density lipoprotein accepts excess cholesterol from peripheral cells and participates in its return to the liver.
notes.D: Chylomicrons chiefly deliver dietary triacylglycerol, and their cholesterol-rich remnants are taken up by the liver.
notes.E: Very-low-density lipoprotein chiefly exports hepatic triacylglycerol and gives rise to cholesterol-enriched particles as it loses fat.

bio-010.why: The liver packages triacylglycerol into very-low-density lipoprotein for export. Lipoprotein lipase then hydrolyses the particle's triacylglycerol in capillaries, making fatty acids available to muscle and adipose tissue.

notes.A: Chylomicrons are rich in triacylglycerol too, but the intestine produces them to transport fat absorbed from a meal.
notes.B: Low-density lipoprotein has already lost much of its precursor's triacylglycerol and is enriched in cholesteryl esters.
notes.D: High-density lipoprotein participates mainly in cholesterol transport and carries a relatively small amount of triacylglycerol.
notes.E: Intermediate-density lipoprotein is the remnant formed after lipoprotein lipase has removed some triacylglycerol from the hepatic particle.

bio-011.why: Acetyl-CoA supplies all the carbon atoms retained in cholesterol. Its two-carbon units first form acetoacetyl-CoA and then HMG-CoA, which is reduced to mevalonate in the sterol pathway.

notes.A: Free acetate must first be activated with coenzyme A before it can enter cholesterol synthesis.
notes.C: Oxaloacetate can help export acetyl units as citrate, but is regenerated when cytosolic citrate is cleaved.
notes.D: Malate participates in the citrate shuttle and can help supply reducing power for biosynthesis.
notes.E: Pyruvate can yield acetyl-CoA through oxidative decarboxylation, placing it upstream of the direct building block.

bio-012.why: Cholecystokinin is made by intestinal endocrine cells from a peptide precursor, preprocholecystokinin. The other choices are sterols or products of sterol metabolism.

notes.A: The liver oxidises and shortens the side chain of cholesterol to form primary bile acids, including chenodeoxycholic acid.
notes.B: Glycocholic acid forms when the liver conjugates the cholesterol-derived bile acid cholic acid with glycine.
notes.C: Steroid-producing cells convert cholesterol to pregnenolone, from which they can synthesise testosterone.
notes.D: In skin, ultraviolet B light acts on the sterol precursor 7-dehydrocholesterol to initiate vitamin D₃ synthesis.

bio-015.why: Type IIa hyperlipoproteinaemia is an isolated elevation of LDL with relatively normal triglycerides. Reduced receptor-mediated LDL clearance is a classic cause, as in familial hypercholesterolaemia due to an impaired LDL receptor pathway.

notes.A: Increased hepatic production of VLDL would usually raise plasma triglycerides rather than producing an isolated increase in LDL cholesterol.
notes.C: High HDL does not explain an isolated accumulation of LDL particles in type IIa hyperlipoproteinaemia.
notes.D: Impaired processing of VLDL would retain more triglyceride-rich particles. It is not the expected mechanism for an isolated LDL elevation.

bio-016.why: Lovastatin inhibits HMG-CoA reductase and decreases hepatic cholesterol synthesis. Lower intracellular cholesterol can increase expression of functioning LDL receptors, increasing LDL clearance and lowering blood cholesterol. The response is smaller when receptor activity is nearly absent.

notes.A: Lower hepatic cholesterol generally increases expression of residual functional LDL receptors through sterol-sensitive regulation.
notes.B: Lovastatin decreases de novo cholesterol synthesis by competitively inhibiting HMG-CoA reductase, even though feedback can increase enzyme expression.
notes.C: ACAT esterifies intracellular cholesterol for storage. Increased esterification is not the principal action of lovastatin.
notes.E: Statins usually lower LDL and can also modestly decrease circulating triglyceride concentrations rather than raising them.

bio-017.why: Lipoprotein density increases as the fraction of protein relative to lipid increases. The order from lowest to highest is chylomicrons, VLDL, IDL, LDL and HDL. The proposed sequences do not follow that order.

notes.A: Chylomicrons are the least dense, but VLDL is less dense than LDL and must come before LDL.
notes.B: HDL has the highest density in this group and follows LDL in the order of increasing density.
notes.C: VLDL is less dense than IDL, because IDL is a smaller remnant left after some triglyceride has been removed.
notes.D: HDL, LDL and VLDL are listed in descending rather than ascending order of density.

bio-020.why: The malonyl/acetyltransferase domain of mammalian fatty acid synthase transfers malonyl from malonyl-CoA to the terminal thiol of ACP's phosphopantetheine arm. The loaded malonyl–ACP supplies a two-carbon unit during condensation.

notes.A: NADPH supplies reducing equivalents for later steps. It does not transfer the malonyl group from CoA.
notes.B: An acyl carrier protein holds the malonyl group as a thioester. The transfer reaction is catalysed by the transferase domain.
notes.C: The mobile ACP arm carries substrates between enzyme sites. Catalysis of malonyl loading requires the distinct transacylase activity.
notes.D: The beta-ketoacyl reductase uses NADPH after condensation to reduce a carbonyl group. It does not load malonyl onto ACP.

bio-022.why: After condensation, beta-ketoacyl–ACP reductase uses NADPH to reduce the beta-keto group to a hydroxyl group. This is the first reduction in the fatty acid synthase elongation cycle.

notes.A: NADPH supplies reducing equivalents, but the reduction also requires beta-ketoacyl–ACP reductase to catalyse hydride transfer.
notes.C: Enoyl–ACP reductase acts later on the carbon–carbon double bond. The keto group requires beta-ketoacyl–ACP reductase.
notes.D: ACP carries the intermediate but is neither the reductase nor the reducing cofactor for the keto group.
notes.E: The cycle has two reduction reactions. The later enoyl reductase is not needed for the initial conversion of the keto group to an alcohol.

bio-023.why: After dehydration makes a trans-enoyl–ACP intermediate, enoyl–ACP reductase uses NADPH to reduce its carbon–carbon double bond. This yields a saturated acyl–ACP ready for another elongation cycle.

notes.A: NADPH donates reducing equivalents, but the enoyl reductase is required to transfer them to the double bond.
notes.B: Beta-ketoacyl–ACP reductase acts earlier on the carbonyl group, before dehydration produces the enoyl intermediate.
notes.D: ACP can hold the enoyl intermediate, but it does not supply reducing equivalents or replace enoyl–ACP reductase.
notes.E: Both reductases use NADPH in the overall cycle. Beta-ketoacyl–ACP reductase acts at a separate earlier step.

bio-024.why: NADPH provides the reducing equivalents for both reductive steps of mammalian fatty acid synthesis. One NADPH reduces the beta-keto group and another reduces the double bond in each elongation cycle.

notes.B: An acyl carrier protein binds and carries growing intermediates. It does not donate the electrons required for reduction.
notes.C: An ACP domain is a carrier with a phosphopantetheine arm, rather than the source of reducing equivalents.
notes.D: The beta-ketoacyl reductase catalyses reduction but obtains the reducing equivalents it transfers from NADPH.
notes.E: The transacylase loads acetyl and malonyl groups. It is not the source of reducing equivalents.

bio-027.why: Type III hyperlipoproteinaemia is caused by defective clearance of cholesterol-rich remnants, often associated with an apoE variant such as apoE2. The accumulated remnant particles carry both triglyceride and cholesterol, so both can be elevated.

notes.A: The intestine can still make chylomicrons after eating. The defect involves clearance of remnant particles rather than absence of chylomicron production.
notes.B: Remnants derived from VLDL can accumulate, so normal VLDL-related lipid handling is not typical of the disorder.
notes.C: Retained triglyceride-rich remnants contribute to elevated triglyceride levels rather than an isolated normal triglyceride result.
notes.D: Cholesterol carried in accumulating remnant particles is often elevated, along with triglycerides.

bio-028.why: In the principal endoplasmic-reticulum elongation system, malonyl-CoA is the immediate donor of the two carbons added to the acyl chain. Acetyl-CoA is upstream as a source of malonyl-CoA, rather than the immediate donor in the elongase reaction.

notes.A: Each elongation round uses condensation, reduction, dehydration and a second reduction, analogous to the sequence of fatty acid synthase.
notes.B: The major elongase system for long-chain acyl-CoAs is associated with the endoplasmic reticulum.
notes.C: One elongation round can convert a 16-carbon palmitoyl-CoA to an 18-carbon product, stearoyl-CoA.
notes.D: Malonyl-CoA is a substrate for the endoplasmic-reticulum elongase and supplies the added carbons after decarboxylation.

bio-030.why: A large meal supplies triglyceride that enterocytes package into chylomicrons. At about three hours after eating, these triglyceride-rich particles can increase circulating triglycerides. LDL and HDL cholesterol usually change less acutely.

notes.B: Postprandial dietary lipid is carried mainly in chylomicrons. A sharp immediate rise in LDL cholesterol is not the characteristic effect.
notes.C: HDL cholesterol usually does not fall sharply after a single meal in a healthy person. Triglyceride-rich particles change more.
notes.D: VLDL is produced in the liver, while the new postprandial particles come from the intestine. A sharp fall in VLDL is not the expected change.

bio-304.why: The Friedewald equation has long been used to estimate LDL cholesterol and can work reasonably in appropriate samples. Its simplifying assumptions can cause error at high triglyceride concentrations or very low LDL. Those limitations do not explain its widespread use.

notes.A: Both statements can be true, but the unmodelled factors explain potential error rather than why the calculation is useful.
notes.C: The equation has practical limitations because the triglyceride-to-cholesterol ratio in VLDL is not constant across samples.
notes.D: The long-standing use of the estimate in appropriate settings is real, even though newer equations can improve accuracy.
notes.E: The estimate is widely used historically, and the concern about unaccounted sources of error is also valid.

bio-305.why: Very high triglycerides can cause acute pancreatitis. A proposed mechanism is that chylomicron-rich blood impairs pancreatic microcirculation and lipases release locally injurious free fatty acids. Ischaemia and local acidosis can reinforce the injury.

notes.B: The reason provides a recognised mechanism that can connect severe triglyceride elevation to pancreatic tissue injury.
notes.C: Capillary flow changes and free-fatty-acid toxicity are plausible contributors to the link, even though they may not account for every case.
notes.D: Severe hypertriglyceridaemia is an established cause of acute pancreatitis, so the assertion is not false.
notes.E: Both the association and the proposed microvascular and lipotoxic explanation have physiological support.

bio-310.why: Vertebrate cytosolic fatty acid synthase is a type I synthase. Each polypeptide contains multiple catalytic domains and an ACP domain, and two polypeptides associate to form the functional complex that commonly produces palmitate.

notes.A: Separate proteins carry out the individual reactions of type II synthase systems. The vertebrate cytosolic enzyme combines the activities in one polypeptide.
notes.B: Cytosolic fatty acid synthase is encoded by a nuclear gene, rather than by the mitochondrial genome.
notes.C: The major pathway for de novo palmitate production is cytosolic. Mitochondria have a distinct specialised synthesis system.
notes.E: Multiple enzyme activities assembled in one protein chain are a defining feature of the vertebrate type I synthase.

bio-313.why: Lovastatin is a statin. Its active form competitively inhibits HMG-CoA reductase, reducing mevalonate formation and hepatic cholesterol synthesis.

notes.A: Clofibrate is a fibrate that acts mainly through PPAR-alpha to change expression of lipid metabolism genes.
notes.B: Gemfibrozil is a fibrate used to lower triglycerides. Its principal mechanism does not involve direct inhibition of HMG-CoA reductase.
notes.D: Cholestyramine binds bile acids in the gut and increases their faecal loss. It does not directly inhibit the reductase.
notes.E: Lovastatin has a well-defined direct inhibitory action at the reductase substrate-binding site.

bio-314.why: Simvastatin inhibits hepatic HMG-CoA reductase, which lowers intracellular cholesterol and increases LDL receptor expression. The resulting decline in circulating LDL reduces the risk of atherosclerotic cardiovascular events.

notes.A: Low-dose niacin is not standard drug therapy for atherosclerotic cardiovascular risk reduction. Lipid effects from pharmacological niacin do not substitute for established statin benefit.
notes.B: High-dose vitamin C is not an established substitute for LDL-lowering therapy to reduce atherosclerotic events.
notes.C: Bariatric surgery can improve some cardiovascular risk factors in selected patients, but it is a procedure rather than the drug treatment asked for.
notes.D: Dietary modification contributes to risk reduction. It is a lifestyle intervention rather than a medication.

bio-317.why: Liver-derived VLDL contains one apoB-100 molecule per particle. ApoB-100 is the structural scaffold and remains with the particle as it is converted to IDL and, for some particles, LDL.

notes.B: ApoB-48 is a shorter product expressed in the intestine and is the structural protein of chylomicrons.
notes.C: ApoA-I is the principal structural apolipoprotein of HDL, rather than the scaffold of VLDL.
notes.D: ApoC-II can be carried on VLDL and activates lipoprotein lipase. It is exchangeable and not the main structural protein.
notes.E: ApoE helps hepatic receptors recognise some triglyceride-rich remnants. It is not the fixed structural scaffold of VLDL.

bio-318.why: Persistently elevated VLDL can increase exposure to atherogenic apoB-containing remnant particles. Smaller VLDL remnants can enter and be retained in the arterial wall, contributing to atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease.

notes.B: VLDL and its remnants carry cholesterol as well as triglyceride. Persistent elevation does not characteristically cause low blood cholesterol.
notes.C: Hepatosplenomegaly can occur in severe chylomicronaemia or other disorders. It is not the principal long-term consequence of chronically raised VLDL.
notes.D: Severe hypertriglyceridaemia can cause abdominal pain from pancreatitis. Atherosclerosis is the key long-term vascular consequence of increased atherogenic remnants.
notes.E: Lipoprotein lipase deficiency can cause triglyceride-rich particles to accumulate. It is a possible underlying disorder, rather than a consequence of increased VLDL.

bio-319.why: Many lipidoses are inherited storage disorders in which a defect in lipid degradation causes particular substrates to accumulate. Demonstration of reduced activity of the relevant enzyme can support the diagnosis, sometimes together with genetic and biomarker tests.

notes.A: Classic lipid storage disorders are usually inherited rather than acquired during life.
notes.B: The substrate typically accumulates because it cannot be degraded normally. Its concentration may rise in affected tissue rather than fall.
notes.C: These disorders can affect nervous tissue, liver and other organs. They do not generally cause ordinary obesity by lipid accumulation in the stomach.
notes.E: Some accumulated lipids or derivatives can be detected in body fluids and serve as useful biomarkers, depending on the disorder.

bio-321.why: Statins lower hepatic cholesterol synthesis and increase expression of functioning hepatic LDL receptors. This increases clearance of circulating LDL and usually lowers LDL cholesterol during treatment.

notes.A: A rise in total blood cholesterol is not the expected response when the major LDL cholesterol fraction is being lowered.
notes.B: Statins act chiefly on cholesterol synthesis and LDL clearance, not by lowering blood glucose.
notes.D: Fatty acid beta-oxidation is a separate pathway. Reduced oxidation is not the usual marker of an effective statin response.
notes.E: Hepatic LDL uptake normally increases during statin treatment, so circulating LDL tends to fall rather than rise.

bio-322.why: ApoC-II normally activates lipoprotein lipase. When apoC-II is deficient, triglycerides in chylomicrons are cleared poorly, producing severe hypertriglyceridaemia. This can resemble inherited lipoprotein lipase deficiency.

notes.A: Type I hyperlipoproteinaemia is defined primarily by accumulation of chylomicrons rather than an isolated postprandial increase in VLDL.
notes.B: Failure to activate lipoprotein lipase impairs removal of circulating triglyceride, so a normal triglyceride level is not the expected hallmark.
notes.D: Chylomicrons carry some cholesterol, but the most characteristic change is a major elevation of triglycerides.
notes.E: Reduced lipoprotein lipase activity decreases triglyceride clearance, so triglyceride-rich particles remain in plasma.

bio-324.why: HDL is richest in protein relative to lipid and has the greatest density among these particles. The density then decreases through LDL and VLDL, with triglyceride-rich chylomicrons least dense.

notes.A: LDL is denser than VLDL and must precede it when the particles are listed from most to least dense.
notes.C: HDL has greater density than LDL and chylomicrons, so it belongs at the beginning rather than after them.
notes.D: VLDL is less dense than LDL and HDL. Chylomicrons are the least dense, so they belong at the end.

bio-391.why: Atherosclerosis is a disease of the intima of medium and large arteries. Retained apoB-containing lipoproteins and subsequent inflammatory and fibrous responses contribute to plaque formation. The defining process does not take place in capillary walls.

notes.A: Both claims misidentify capillaries as the site of disease. Plaques form in the arterial intima rather than beneath an outer capillary lining.
notes.B: The vessel and layer descriptions are both inaccurate, so neither claim supplies a valid explanation.
notes.C: Plaque-related thickening involves arteries, not capillaries. The assertion therefore misstates the affected vessels.
notes.D: Lipid retention occurs in the arterial intima. The reason is also inaccurate because it places the lesion in capillaries.

bio-443.why: A total plasma cholesterol above 7.0 mmol/L is markedly elevated among these choices. Clinical decisions also depend on the LDL cholesterol value, family history and other findings, rather than total cholesterol alone.

notes.B: Low bile acid concentrations can affect intestinal fat handling. They are not a plasma cholesterol measurement.
notes.C: Fat malabsorption can result from several digestive disorders. It does not itself indicate markedly elevated plasma cholesterol.
notes.D: HMG-CoA reductase participates in cholesterol synthesis. Deficiency of the enzyme is not a measured high cholesterol level.
notes.E: An absence of a heart attack does not exclude high plasma cholesterol. Cholesterol is measured directly.

bio-444.why: Bile salts help stabilise small lipid droplets and form mixed micelles that carry lipid digestion products. Low delivery of bile salts to the intestine can impair emulsification and make fat absorption less efficient.

notes.A: High plasma cholesterol measures a circulating lipid concentration. It does not show that too few bile salts reach the intestinal lumen.
notes.C: Impaired fat absorption can follow defective emulsification. It is a possible result rather than the upstream loss of an emulsifying agent.
notes.D: HMG-CoA reductase is part of cholesterol synthesis, but the most direct defect here is reduced intestinal availability of bile salts.
notes.E: The absence of a heart attack does not explain how dietary fat is dispersed in the intestine.

bio-445.why: Poor emulsification can limit access of lipases to dietary fat and can accompany insufficient mixed-micelle formation. This reduces absorption of long-chain lipid products and can lead to fatty stools and fat-soluble vitamin malabsorption.

notes.A: Defective emulsification directly affects intestinal lipid processing. A high plasma cholesterol level is not its expected presentation.
notes.B: A low bile salt supply can cause defective emulsification. It is an upstream factor rather than the resulting problem with nutrient uptake.
notes.D: HMG-CoA reductase is involved in cholesterol synthesis. Deficient activity is not a clinical manifestation diagnostic of low emulsification.
notes.E: The absence of a heart attack does not indicate whether dietary fat is being digested and absorbed.

bio-458.why: Carrots are plant foods and are not a meaningful dietary source of cholesterol. Plant tissues primarily contain phytosterols. Butter, cheese and egg yolk are animal foods that contribute cholesterol.

notes.A: Butter contains dairy fat and can provide dietary cholesterol, although the amount depends on the serving.
notes.B: Cheese is made from milk and contains some cholesterol, with variation according to fat content and serving size.
notes.C: Egg yolk contains cholesterol in its lipid fraction, in contrast to typical plant foods.

bio-903.why: Bile salts are derived from cholesterol. Hepatocytes convert the sterol into primary bile acids, which can be conjugated with glycine or taurine before secretion into bile.

notes.B: Gangliosides are glycosphingolipids built from ceramide and an oligosaccharide that contains sialic acid.
notes.C: Geraniol is a monoterpene alcohol formed from isoprenoid precursors. It is not made by modifying a sterol.
notes.D: Phosphatidylglycerol is a glycerophospholipid with a glycerol head group. Its backbone is not cholesterol.
notes.E: Prostaglandins are eicosanoids formed from polyunsaturated fatty acids, often arachidonic acid.

bio-904.why: Statins competitively inhibit HMG-CoA reductase, slowing conversion of HMG-CoA to mevalonate. Lower hepatic cholesterol increases LDL receptor expression, which promotes removal of LDL from blood.

notes.B: Lipoprotein lipase hydrolyses triglycerides in circulating particles. It is not the direct enzyme target of statins.
notes.C: The direct drug effect is inhibition of the reductase, even though feedback can increase expression of the enzyme.
notes.D: Lower plasma LDL reflects increased hepatic clearance through LDL receptors. Direct blockade of LDL particle synthesis is not the main mechanism.
notes.E: Some statins modestly change HDL cholesterol, but inhibition of HMG-CoA reductase is the defining drug action.

bio-031.why: Antioxidants inhibit oxidation by removing reactive species, interrupting radical chain reactions or preventing reactive species from forming. The exact mechanism depends on the particular antioxidant.

notes.A: A substance that promotes radical formation is acting as a pro-oxidant under those conditions.

bio-032.why: Antioxidant activity depends on a compound's structure and on conditions around it. The local redox state, oxygen availability and transition metals can change which reactions occur and whether the compound has a net antioxidant effect.

notes.A: Molecular structure affects how readily a compound can donate electrons, stabilise a radical or enter a particular cellular compartment.
notes.B: The local redox state can affect whether the compound is available in a form that scavenges reactive species or is regenerated after reacting.
notes.C: Oxygen and transition metals influence radical formation and can change the net effect of a compound in a particular environment.

bio-033.why: Free radicals can damage many classes of cell molecules. They initiate lipid peroxidation, oxidise proteins and carbohydrates, and modify DNA bases or the sugar–phosphate backbone.

notes.A: Radicals can attack polyunsaturated fatty acids and initiate a chain reaction of membrane lipid peroxidation.
notes.B: Oxidative attack can modify carbohydrates, including the deoxyribose backbone in DNA and sugars in other cell structures.
notes.C: Oxidation can modify amino acid side chains and alter the structure, stability or activity of proteins.
notes.D: Reactive species can modify DNA bases and contribute to strand breaks or other lesions.

bio-034.why: Carotenoids have extended systems of conjugated double bonds. These allow them to accept excitation energy from singlet oxygen and dissipate it, usually as heat, returning oxygen toward its ground state.

notes.A: How widely a pigment occurs in nature does not explain its molecular capacity to quench singlet oxygen.
notes.C: Methyl groups can influence overall structure, but the extended conjugated system is the key feature for efficient energy transfer.
notes.D: The conjugated electron system provides a recognised mechanism for singlet oxygen quenching.

bio-035.why: Antioxidant systems limit damage by removing reactive oxygen species or interrupting the reactions they start. This can protect cell components without blocking the ordinary use of oxygen in aerobic metabolism.

notes.A: Antioxidants do not generally block aerobic pathways by binding molecular oxygen. They target specific reactive intermediates or their reactions.
notes.B: Deliberately increasing radical formation is a pro-oxidant effect. It is not the usual protective action of antioxidants.
notes.D: Some vitamins themselves participate in antioxidant systems. Generating reactive oxygen species by complexing with vitamins is not the general mechanism.

bio-037.why: Superoxide dismutase converts superoxide to hydrogen peroxide and molecular oxygen. Catalase and peroxidases then remove hydrogen peroxide, so water is not the direct product of superoxide dismutase.

notes.A: Mitochondrial electron transfer can reduce oxygen one electron at a time and produce superoxide.
notes.B: Superoxide has an unpaired electron and is classified as a radical reactive oxygen species.
notes.D: Superoxide can participate in metal-catalysed production of hydroxyl radical from hydrogen peroxide. The direct uncatalysed reaction is very slow.

bio-039.why: Red cells use G6PD to generate NADPH and maintain reduced glutathione. Certain oxidant antimalarials can trigger haemolysis in people with G6PD deficiency, causing dark urine from free haemoglobin. Malaria itself can also cause haemolysis.

notes.A: Acute nephritis can cause dark urine from red cells in the urine. The timing after an oxidant exposure raises concern for haemolysis in this vignette.
notes.C: Hepatitis can darken urine through conjugated bilirubin, but that differs mechanistically from the possible haemoglobinuria after oxidative red-cell injury.
notes.D: Haematuria means intact red cells are present in urine. Intravascular haemolysis can instead release free haemoglobin into urine.

bio-042.why: Glutathione reductase uses NADPH to reduce the disulphide bond of oxidised glutathione. This regenerates two reduced glutathione molecules for use in antioxidant reactions.

notes.A: Glutathione peroxidase uses reduced glutathione to remove peroxides, forming oxidised glutathione in the process.
notes.B: The standard enzyme that regenerates reduced glutathione from its disulphide is glutathione reductase. This reaction uses NADPH.
notes.D: Glutathione synthetase forms glutathione by adding glycine during biosynthesis. It does not reduce oxidised glutathione.

bio-043.why: Myeloperoxidase uses hydrogen peroxide and chloride to produce hypochlorous acid in phagocytes. Its characteristic role is to generate a reactive antimicrobial oxidant, unlike antioxidant systems that remove superoxide or peroxides.

notes.A: Glutathione peroxidase uses reduced glutathione to remove hydrogen peroxide or lipid hydroperoxides.
notes.B: Catalase converts hydrogen peroxide to water and oxygen, limiting peroxide accumulation.
notes.C: Superoxide dismutase converts the superoxide radical to hydrogen peroxide and oxygen so other enzymes can handle the peroxide.

bio-044.why: Glutathione is a reducing substrate rather than the catalyst. Glutathione peroxidase catalyses peroxide reduction using reduced glutathione, which is oxidised in the process.

notes.A: Different superoxide dismutase forms occur in the cytosol and mitochondria, protecting those cellular compartments.
notes.B: Dismutation of superoxide produces hydrogen peroxide and molecular oxygen.
notes.C: Catalase removes hydrogen peroxide through a reaction that produces water and molecular oxygen.

bio-045.why: DNA can be damaged by reactive oxygen species. Oxidation can generate modified bases such as 8-oxoguanine and contribute to strand breaks, so antioxidant defences and DNA repair are important.

notes.A: Healthy cells have systems that balance the production and removal of reactive species and maintain a suitable redox environment.
notes.B: Mitochondrial metabolism can generate hydrogen peroxide, some of which can reach the cytosol and participate in redox signalling.
notes.C: The KEAP1–NRF2 system senses changes in oxidative and electrophilic stress and regulates expression of protective genes.

bio-046.why: The hydroxyl radical reacts extremely rapidly with many nearby molecules, including lipids, proteins and DNA. It often causes damage near the site where it forms because its lifetime is so short.

notes.B: Superoxide is a radical that participates in redox reactions, but it is generally less reactive toward many targets than hydroxyl radical.
notes.C: Hydrogen peroxide is a reactive oxygen species but not a free radical because it has no unpaired electron.
notes.D: Organic oxygen-centred radicals can participate in oxidative reactions. Hydroxyl radical is usually the most rapidly reacting species among these choices.

bio-047.why: Different antioxidants protect different compartments or act at different stages of oxidation. Some remove peroxides, while others interrupt lipid radical chains or regenerate the active form of another antioxidant.

notes.B: A single antioxidant does not protect equally against all oxidants or in every cellular compartment.

bio-048.why: Oxidative stress can damage proteins, nucleic acids or other targets without producing detectable lipid peroxidation. The absence of one marker therefore does not rule out redox imbalance.

notes.B: Lipid peroxidation is only one potential result of oxidative stress. Other targets can be damaged even when this marker is absent.

bio-050.why: Lipid peroxidation can produce reactive aldehydes that form DNA adducts or alter signalling. These effects can contribute to mutations or processes associated with tumour development, although peroxidation alone does not determine whether cancer occurs.

notes.B: Lipid peroxidation can have effects beyond the membrane. Its reactive products can modify DNA and participate in processes that contribute to oncogenesis.

bio-052.why: DNA injury can activate cellular stress pathways that change mitochondrial or enzyme activity and lead to additional reactive oxygen species. Oxidative species can also cause DNA damage, so the association can operate in both directions.

notes.B: DNA damage is not only an outcome of oxidative stress. A damage response can also increase oxidant generation in some settings.

bio-053.why: Reactive oxygen species can arise during normal metabolism, including mitochondrial electron transfer. Disease and tissue injury can increase their formation through inflammatory or metal-catalysed reactions, including reactions involving hydrogen peroxide.

notes.A: Normal metabolism is a source, but disease and tissue injury can also change oxidant production.
notes.B: Endogenous metabolism and peroxide-related reactions are relevant, and damaged tissue can also contribute to reactive species formation.
notes.C: A focus on disease and damage omits the low-level oxidant production that occurs in normal cellular metabolism.
notes.D: Normal metabolism and injured tissue are sources. Hydrogen peroxide can also give rise to more reactive species through metal-catalysed reactions.

bio-054.why: Reactive oxygen species can originate in several cellular compartments. Mitochondrial electron transfer is a common source, while oxidant-generating enzymes and redox reactions can contribute in the cytoplasm and nuclear region.

notes.A: The nucleus can experience local generation of oxidants, but mitochondria and cytosolic reactions can also contribute.
notes.B: Mitochondria are a major source, but reactive oxygen species are not generated exclusively in mitochondria.
notes.C: Nuclear and mitochondrial sources are possible. Cytoplasmic enzyme reactions can also contribute to oxidant formation.
notes.D: Cytoplasmic and mitochondrial sources are well recognised. Redox-active processes in the nuclear region can also generate reactive species.

bio-055.why: Coffee contains phenolic compounds, almonds provide vitamin E, and many mushrooms contain compounds such as ergothioneine. Each can supply substances with antioxidant properties, although amounts and biological effects differ.

notes.A: Coffee contributes compounds such as chlorogenic acids. Almonds and mushrooms also contain compounds with antioxidant properties.
notes.B: Coffee and almonds both contribute antioxidant compounds, and some mushrooms are a dietary source of ergothioneine.
notes.C: Almonds and mushrooms supply antioxidant compounds. Coffee also contains phenolic substances rather than supplying caffeine alone.
notes.D: Coffee and mushrooms contribute antioxidant compounds. Almonds are also a source of vitamin E and other dietary antioxidants.
